overview.text: A polar covalent bond forms when two atoms share bonding electrons, but one attracts the shared electron cloud more strongly because it has higher electronegativity. The sharing remains covalent rather than involving complete electron transfer, yet the unequal distribution gives the atoms partial charges: δ− on the electron-richer atom and δ+ on the other. In methanol’s C–O bond, for example, oxygen pulls electron density away from carbon. Hydrogen chloride also has a polar covalent bond; its measurable dipole reflects charge separation, not a full electron transferred. Bond polarity helps describe the continuum between covalent and ionic bonding, and generally increases as the electronegativity difference grows.

key_facts.text: Electronegativity describes an atom’s ability to attract shared bonding electrons; a difference between bonded atoms causes unequal sharing.
The more electron-attracting atom is labeled δ−, and the other atom δ+; these are partial charges, not full ionic charges.
A C–O bond in methanol is polar: oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than carbon.
A bond dipole describes charge separation; in HCl, the electron distribution favors chlorine, while hydrogen is partially positive.
A molecule’s dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles, so bond polarity and whole-molecule polarity are related but distinct ideas.
